title: Consult your heart
hook: righteousness is good character, and sin is what wavers in your chest (Nawawi 27, al-Nawwas and Wabisah)
tomorrow: a talk so moving the listeners cried. what did they ask for next?

segments.voice: Yesterday: every joint owes charity, every joint, every day, a debt paid in peace and lifted bags. Today, the question under all of it: how do you know what's right?

Where do you look when nobody can tell you what's right? The forums disagree. The friends disagree. Some questions are too small or too new for a rulebook, and the rules don't quite reach this exact case. Wabisah came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, meaning to ask about righteousness and sin, and before he could, he was asked: you've come to ask about righteousness? Then came the answer, and it didn't point to a book or a crowd. It pointed inward: consult your heart.
screen: `THE FORUMS DISAGREE.` → `THE RULES DON'T QUITE REACH.` → `CONSULT YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Al-Nawawi's twenty-seventh hadith comes in two tellings. To al-Nawwas, in Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase: righteousness is good character, and sin is what wavers in your chest and you'd hate for people to find out. To Wabisah: consult your heart. Righteousness is what the soul is at rest with; sin is what churns in the chest, even if people give you ruling after ruling. So the question, what's right, gets this answer: the heart has a voice. Not a mood. A settled place, and a churn, and you can learn to tell them apart. The hadith even gives the churn a test: it's the thing you'd hate for people to find out. Now a neighbor. Christians read something close in Paul's letter to the Romans. He writes of people who "shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness." Same picture: a law written inside, and a witness that speaks up. And one honest difference. Paul's line sits inside a longer argument about Jews, Gentiles and God's judgment. The hadith is a working test for one choice, here and now, and the heart it consults is one that already knows the revealed limits. Two traditions pointing inward, neither ranked, and neither asks you to switch the heart off. Ask your heart.
screen: `RIGHTEOUSNESS: GOOD CHARACTER.` · `SIN: WHAT CHURNS IN THE CHEST.` · `PAUL: A LAW WRITTEN IN HEARTS.` · `A WORKING TEST, NOT A MOOD.` · then, large: `ASK YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and rest one hand on your chest. Bring up one choice in front of you this week, and hold each option there for a few breaths, one at a time. Notice which one settles and which one churns; nothing has to be decided yet. The hand is only a way of listening.
Consult your heart: istafti qalbak, ask your heart for a ruling. What it rests with is righteousness; what churns is sin.
For the road: ask your heart, because the churn is telling you something worth hearing. Hadith twenty-seven, heard.

howItsDone: Muslims quote 'istafti qalbak' for gray areas, usually alongside learning the law and asking people of knowledge, not instead of them.

fork.reveal: 'even if people give you ruling after ruling': the hadith sets the heart's churn above the crowd's permission.

original.note: Arabic: consult your heart; literally, ask your heart for a ruling.

trapdoor: what you thought: just follow your heart.
what it means: the settled heart, alongside the law, is a test: what it rests with is righteousness; what churns is sin.
what a scholar hears: Sahih Muslim 2553 (al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an) and the Wabisah report in Musnad Ahmad and Sunan al-Darimi, which al-Nawawi graded hasan.
guess: ask the settled heart: what rests, what churns

chat.meaning: The hadith: sin is what wavers in your chest and you'd hate people to find out. The churn is the heart answering.
